blocks.text: Manasseh's account in Second Chronicles records a striking reversal. After decades of leading Judah into systematic idolatry—rebuilding pagan high places, installing altars in the Temple itself, practicing child sacrifice, and engaging in divination and sorcery—he was captured by Assyrian forces and carried into exile. This captivity became the occasion for transformation. In his distress, Manasseh sought the LORD his God and humbled himself greatly before the God of his fathers. Through prayer, he experienced divine restoration: God returned him to Jerusalem, where Manasseh underwent genuine religious reform, recognizing God's lordship over the kingdom.

sections.title: Manasseh's Story Within Chronicles' Theological Vision

blocks.text: The cycle of seeking the LORD, humbling oneself, praying, and turning from apostasy appears repeatedly across the narratives of Judah's kings in Chronicles. Manasseh's experience exemplifies this pattern: his profound transgression and subsequent distress prompted genuine repentance, which God met with restoration. This recurring theological perspective—that even severe rebellion against God need not be final if accompanied by sincere humility and prayer—shapes the Chronicler's interpretation of the kingdom's history. The pattern emphasizes the possibility of reversal and reform within the covenant relationship between God and Judah's monarchy.
